top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross- sectional studies were included in the meta- analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta- analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.text: Two authors independently conducted systematic searches in the following databases: Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed. top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: ⇒ This is the first systematic review and meta- analysis exclusively focused on the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS in children and adolescents. For numbered affiliations see end of article. Results A total of eight studies involving children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years were included in the meta- analysis (n=6562, 50% girls). Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%). Conclusion This meta- analysis suggested that increased adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with lower probabilities of having cardiometabolic risk among children and adolescents. Thus, our findings suggest that public health strategies are needed to implement and promote effective actions toward healthy eating habits in children and adolescents. ⇒ Low adherence to the MedDiet is significantly associated with increased odds of having MetS among youth (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.45 to 3.28).

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross- sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta- analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: The characteristics of the eight studies included in this meta- analysis are presented in table 2. All studies were cross- sectional in design and published between 2011 and 2022. The studies were conducted in diverse geographic settings, including Europe (Spain, Greece, Italy), the Middle East (Iran), the USA and Turkey. The sample sizes ranged from 137 to 1972 participants, with the proportion of female participants ranging from 47.5% to 60.5%. Figure 1 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analyses flowchart. There was considerable heterogeneity in the age of participants across studies, ranging from 6 to 19 years, covering both early and late adolescence. Dietary adherence to the MedDiet was assessed via different tools: five studies employed the KIDMED index, whereas three used FFQs to derive MedDiet scores or patterns. The KIDMED is a validated, structured index specifically designed to measure adherence to the MedDiet in young populations and is based on a 16- item scoring system. In contrast, FFQs are broader tools used to assess usual dietary intake, from which MedDiet adherence scores are derived using predefined criteria. Similarly, outcome measures varied, with most studies using International Diabetes Federation (IDF) criteria for defining MetS, while some also included definitions based on homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA- IR) or other phenotype- based approaches (eg, metabolically unhealthy obesity [MUO]). The main results consistently indicated an inverse association between adherence to the MedDiet and the presence of MetS or its components, although FFQ, food frequency questionnaire; HOMA- IR, Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance; IDF , International Diabetes Federation; KIDMED, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index in children and adolescents; MDS, Mediterranean diet score; MedDiet, Mediterranean diet; MetS, metabolic syndrome; MUO, metabolically unhealthy obesity; p , statistical significance. one study did not find a statistically significant association.

top_evidence.text: A meta- analysis was also conducted to investigate the associations between MetS and MedDiet adherence. To determine the overall estimated OR and its related 95% CIs, the random- effects inverse variance model with the traditional DerSimonian and Laird method was used. To measure the percentage of disparities across studies, we used the inconsistency index ( I 2 ), which was calculated with the Cochran Q statistic. I 2 values of 0%-40%, 30%-60%, 50%-90% and 75%--100% were considered cut- off values for non- important, moderate, substantial and considerable degrees of inconsistency, respectively. 30

All results from each study that were compatible with each outcome domain were included. In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.

The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Adolescence and childhood are critical periods for the development of metabolic health, 1 as there are times when changes in diet and lifestyle can have long- term effects on health outcomes. 2 Poor metabolic health in adolescence can lead to the development of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity in adulthood. 3-6 The prevalence of metabolic disorders is increasing globally, especially among adolescents, and this has become a public health concern. 2 7 ⇒ Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies to assess causality and inform evidence- based dietary guidelines for paediatric populations. Check for updates The main features of metabolic health include ideal levels of blood sugar, triglycerides, high- density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, blood pressure and waist circumference. 8-11 Abnormalities in these metabolic health levels can lead to obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and insulin resistance. 4 12 13 The key contributing factors include diet and behaviour, such as an increased intake of foods containing high amounts of saturated fat and carbohydrates, particularly sweetened beverages; a lack of physical activity; and smoking. 1 7 9 14 The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises the significant impact of diet on disease risk and has developed a Global Action Plan to address unhealthy dietary patterns. 15 The plan aims to reduce behavioural risk factors such as physical inactivity, tobacco use, harmful alcohol consumption and unhealthy eating habits. The WHO recommends various dietary changes to promote better health, including maintaining balanced energy intake, limiting saturated and trans fats, transitioning to unsaturated fats, increasing fruit and vegetable intake, and reducing sugar and salt consumption. These recommendations are often found in regional diets, such as the Mediterranean diet (MedDiet), which is characterised by high consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, and olive oil and low consumption of red and processed meats, sweets and refined grains. 16 © Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2025. Re- use permitted under CC BY- NC. No commercial re- use. See rights and permissions. Published by BMJ Group. BMJGroup A MedDiet has been associated with improved metabolic syndrome (MetS) outcomes, including a decreased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity, among adults. 17 Several studies have associated the MedDiet with individual MetS- related factors (blood sugar, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, blood pressure and waist circumference). 14 17-19 A recent meta- analysis highlighted that interventions based on a MedDiet are highly effective in lowering childhood and adolescent obesity and body mass index. 20 However, the extent to which different levels of adherence to the MedDiet are associated with MetS outcomes in youth remains poorly understood. While several studies have reported associations, the consistency and strength of these findings across varying adherence categories warrant further synthesis and evaluation. Several studies have investigated the associations between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS outcomes among adolescents, 21-26 but the results have been inconsistent. Some studies have shown a positive association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS risk, 21-26 whereas others have reported no significant association. 27 To our knowledge, no previous systematic review or meta- analysis has synthesised the available evidence examining the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta- analysis was to investigate whether adherence to a MedDiet is associated with MetS in this population.

These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

The sample sizes ranged from 137 to 1972 participants, with the proportion of female participants ranging from 47.5% to 60.5%. Figure 1 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analyses flowchart. There was considerable heterogeneity in the age of participants across studies, ranging from 6 to 19 years, covering both early and late adolescence. Dietary adherence to the MedDiet was assessed via different tools: five studies employed the KIDMED index, whereas three used FFQs to derive MedDiet scores or patterns. The KIDMED is a validated, structured index specifically designed to measure adherence to the MedDiet in young populations and is based on a 16- item scoring system. In contrast, FFQs are broader tools used to assess usual dietary intake, from which MedDiet adherence scores are derived using predefined criteria. Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross- sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta- analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

top_evidence.text: A search strategy was used to identify all eligible studies published before 22 April 2024. The following terms related to the MedDiet were used: MEDdiet, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index for Children and Adolescents (KIDMED) score, MedDiet score, MedDiet and hypertension, MedDiet and diabetes, KIDMED and MedDiet score. top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: The characteristics of the eight studies included in this meta- analysis are presented in table 2. All studies were cross- sectional in design and published between 2011 and 2022. The studies were conducted in diverse geographic settings, including Europe (Spain, Greece, Italy), the Middle East (Iran), the USA and Turkey. The sample sizes ranged from 137 to 1972 participants, with the proportion of female participants ranging from 47.5% to 60.5%. Figure 1 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analyses flowchart. There was considerable heterogeneity in the age of participants across studies, ranging from 6 to 19 years, covering both early and late adolescence. Dietary adherence to the MedDiet was assessed via different tools: five studies employed the KIDMED index, whereas three used FFQs to derive MedDiet scores or patterns. The KIDMED is a validated, structured index specifically designed to measure adherence to the MedDiet in young populations and is based on a 16- item scoring system. In contrast, FFQs are broader tools used to assess usual dietary intake, from which MedDiet adherence scores are derived using predefined criteria. Similarly, outcome measures varied, with most studies using International Diabetes Federation (IDF) criteria for defining MetS, while some also included definitions based on homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA- IR) or other phenotype- based approaches (eg, metabolically unhealthy obesity [MUO]). The main results consistently indicated an inverse association between adherence to the MedDiet and the presence of MetS or its components, although FFQ, food frequency questionnaire; HOMA- IR, Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance; IDF , International Diabetes Federation; KIDMED, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index in children and adolescents; MDS, Mediterranean diet score; MedDiet, Mediterranean diet; MetS, metabolic syndrome; MUO, metabolically unhealthy obesity; p , statistical significance. one study did not find a statistically significant association.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross- sectional studies were included in the meta- analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta- analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross- sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta- analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: The results of the individual studies are presented in figure 2. Children and adolescents with low adherence to the MedDiet had greater odds of developing MetS compared to those with medium to high adherence. The OR for this association was 2.18, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.45 to 3.28 ( p < 0.001). The inconsistency among the studies, as assessed by the I² statistic, was 64.15%.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.text: The results of the individual studies are presented in figure 2. Children and adolescents with low adherence to the MedDiet had greater odds of developing MetS compared to those with medium to high adherence. top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross- sectional studies were included in the meta- analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta- analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: Figure 4 Sensitivity analysis. CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio. meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted. Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non- Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross- sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well- designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta- analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross- sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review. Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta- analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations. The results of this systematic review and meta- analysis are important from the public health perspective for this specific population since, during the process of growth, various nutritional needs must be met to sustain constant body changes. 32 In addition, healthy behaviours play a key role at early ages and must be promoted, as healthy eating behaviours can extend from childhood into adulthood, 32 helping individuals avoid and prevent obesity and health- related problems. Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega- 3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes. In conclusion, the MedDiet could be a protective factor against MetS among children and adolescents. These findings highlight the potential benefits of the MedDiet for promoting MetS early in life and may have important implications for public health policies and interventions aimed at improving the dietary patterns of children and adolescents. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms and long- term effects of adherence to the MedDiet on MetS in this population.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: A search strategy was used to identify all eligible studies published before 22 April 2024. The search strategy included controlled vocabulary terms specific to each database along with keywords derived from scoping index articles relevant to this meta- analysis. The following terms related to the MedDiet were used: MEDdiet, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index for Children and Adolescents (KIDMED) score, MedDiet score, MedDiet and hypertension, MedDiet and diabetes, KIDMED and MedDiet score. The following outcome terms related to MetS were included: MetS or components (hyperlipidaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, hypertension) combined with health. top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross- sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta- analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.
