elements.quote: A MedDiet has been associated with improved metabolic syndrome (MetS) outcomes, including a decreased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity, among adults. However, the extent to which different levels of adherence to the MedDiet are associated with MetS outcomes in youth remains poorly understood. Several studies have investigated the associations between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS outcomes among adolescents, 21-26 but the results have been inconsistent.
elements.reason: Summarizes existing adult evidence and prior adolescent studies, and explicitly notes key uncertainties (poorly understood associations and inconsistent findings in youth).

elements.quote: The prevalence of metabolic disorders is increasing globally, especially among adolescents, and this has become a public health concern. To our knowledge, no previous systematic review or meta- analysis has synthesised the available evidence examining the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta- analysis was to investigate whether adherence to a MedDiet is associated with MetS in this population.
elements.reason: Explains the public health importance and the need for this review due to the absence of prior syntheses focused on children/adolescents.
The authors state that no previous systematic review or meta-analysis has synthesized this association in children/adolescents, so explaining overlap with similar reviews does not apply.
This is not a review of intervention effects; eligibility included observational longitudinal and cross-sectional designs only.
A logic model for complex interventions is not applicable because the review synthesizes observational associations rather than complex intervention delivery.

elements.quote: All studies were included in the meta- analysis to assess the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: An explicit objective is stated and reflects a PEO-style framework (Population: children and adolescents; Exposure: adherence to the Mediterranean diet; Outcome: metabolic syndrome). However, it is not presented as a structured question/objective using a named question-formulation framework and lacks full structured detail.

The review synthesizes observational (cross-sectional) studies on associations, not intervention effects; thus PICO comparisons do not apply. Evidence: “A total of eight cross- sectional studies were included in the meta- analysis.” (text_17).

elements.quote: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross- sectional study design.
elements.reason: Specifies key study characteristics for eligibility (population, exposure assessment, outcome, and eligible designs) and broadly states setting (all countries/ethnicities). However, no follow-up requirements are described for longitudinal designs, so not all aspects are fully specified.

elements.quote: we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English.

No statement distinguishes exclusions due to outcomes not being measured from exclusions due to outcome results not being reported.

elements.quote: Adolescence and childhood are critical periods for the development of metabolic health, 1 as there are times when changes in diet and lifestyle can have long-term effects on health outcomes. Poor metabolic health in adolescence can lead to the development of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity in adulthood. The prevalence of metabolic disorders is increasing globally, especially among adolescents, and this has become a public health concern. The main features of metabolic health include ideal levels of blood sugar, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, blood pressure and waist circumference. Abnormalities in these metabolic health levels can lead to obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and insulin resistance. The key contributing factors include diet and behaviour, such as an increased intake of foods containing high amounts of saturated fat and carbohydrates, particularly sweetened beverages; a lack of physical activity; and smoking. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises the significant impact of diet on disease risk and has developed a Global Action Plan to address unhealthy dietary patterns. The plan aims to reduce behavioural risk factors such as physical inactivity, tobacco use, harmful alcohol consumption and unhealthy eating habits. The WHO recommends various dietary changes to promote better health, including maintaining balanced energy intake, limiting saturated and trans fats, transitioning to unsaturated fats, increasing fruit and vegetable intake, and reducing sugar and salt consumption. These recommendations are often found in regional diets, such as the Mediterranean diet (MedDiet), which is characterised by high consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, and olive oil and low consumption of red and processed meats, sweets and refined grains. A MedDiet has been associated with improved metabolic syndrome (MetS) outcomes, including a decreased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity, among adults. Several studies have associated the MedDiet with individual MetS-related factors (blood sugar, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, blood pressure and waist circumference). A recent meta-analysis highlighted that interventions based on a MedDiet are highly effective in lowering childhood and adolescent obesity and body mass index.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge regarding metabolic health, dietary factors, and the Mediterranean diet (MedDiet), including its associations with metabolic syndrome (MetS) outcomes in adults and children. It highlights important uncertainties by noting inconsistent findings in previous studies on MedDiet adherence and MetS in adolescents.

elements.quote: However, the extent to which different levels of adherence to the MedDiet are associated with MetS outcomes in youth remains poorly understood. While several studies have reported associations, the consistency and strength of these findings across varying adherence categories warrant further synthesis and evaluation. Several studies have investigated the associations between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS outcomes among adolescents, but the results have been inconsistent. Some studies have shown a positive association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS risk, whereas others have reported no significant association. To our knowledge, no previous systematic review or meta-analysis has synthesised the available evidence examining the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to investigate whether adherence to a MedDiet is associated with MetS in this population.
elements.reason: The text explains the importance and need for conducting the review by emphasizing the lack of synthesis on the association between MedDiet adherence and MetS in children and adolescents, despite existing inconsistent studies. It also highlights the aim of the review to address this gap.

elements.quote: Conversely, this study has certain strengths. For example, to our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta-analysis that examined the association between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. In addition, our study included studies that employed validated MedDiet adherence scores to assess adherence to the MedDiet, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our findings. Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al, our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well-designed systematic review and meta-analysis of paediatric populations.
elements.reason: The text explicitly identifies and cites a previous systematic review (Bakaloudi et al) that examined MedDiet adherence and MetS in adults, explaining the need for the current review focused on children and adolescents.

elements.quote: Several potential mechanisms may explain the observed association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS. 11 25 33 The MedDiet is characterised by a high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds and healthy fats (such as olive oil and fish) and a moderate intake of dairy products, poultry and eggs, with limited intake of red meat and processed foods. 34 35 The high intake of fruits and vegetables, whole grains and legumes provides important sources of dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, which may help reduce inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance and improve insulin sensitivity. 18 36 Healthy fats in the MedDiet, such as monounsaturated fats from olive oil and omega-3 fatty acids from fish, may also have beneficial effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation and glucose homeostasis. 36 In addition, the MedDiet is typically low in added sugars and highly processed foods, which may contribute to improved MetS outcomes.
